summary: Describes an optional, backward-compatible IS-IS extension that allows flood reflection topologies, where Level 1 areas provide transit for Level 2 using L2 flood reflection adjacencies. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: Instead of every router telling every other router everything, some routers relay news for the rest, which keeps things simpler in big networks.

questions: how to reduce l2 full mesh in is-is
what is flood reflection in is-is
how does flood reflection scale is-is networks
subtitle: A scalability technique for multi-area IS-IS networks using flood reflectors.

tldr.problem: In multi-area IS-IS networks that need a single Level 2 backbone spanning many routers, the control plane overhead of maintaining a full mesh of Level 2 adjacencies between border routers becomes impractical, limiting scalability.
tldr.mechanism: Flood reflection creates a star topology at the control plane: border routers build Level 2 adjacencies only to designated flood reflector routers, which reflood Level 2 information. Meanwhile, forwarding can still use the full Level 1 topology through tunnels or reachability redistribution.
tldr.outcome: Networks can scale to larger Level 2 domains with fewer control plane adjacencies and state. The technique is backward-compatible and requires changes only on routers participating in flood reflection, enabling incremental deployment.

facts.label: Adjacency growth (flood reflection)
facts.value: Linear (R*n, where R = reflectors, n = clients)

facts.label: Reflector redundancy
facts.value: Multiple reflectors supported, no synchronization needed

today: RFC 9377 is an Experimental protocol published in April 2023. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains available for experimental implementations and evaluation by network operators deploying or considering multi-area IS-IS networks.

sections.title: Scaling Multi-Area IS-IS Networks
sections.content:
IS-IS is a routing protocol with two levels: Level 1 (L1) handles routing within areas, and Level 2 (L2) is the backbone connecting those areas. For networks where a single flat Level 2 domain needs to span many routers, the control plane becomes the bottleneck. Each router must maintain adjacencies to every other L2 router, resulting in a quadratic growth of state: a 20-router L2 domain requires 190 adjacencies in a full mesh.

Flood reflection solves this by allowing Level 1 areas to provide transit for Level 2 traffic without every L1/L2 border router needing a direct Level 2 adjacency to every other border router. Instead, border routers build Level 2 adjacencies only to designated flood reflectors within the same Level 1 area. The flood reflectors reflood Level 2 information, connecting the separate Level 2 islands. A network with 20 border routers and 2 flood reflectors requires only 40 L2 adjacencies, compared to 190 in a flat design.

The technique mirrors BGP route reflection: the flood reflectors participate in the control plane (propagating routing information) but are not required to carry data traffic. This separation of control plane and forwarding plane is the key to achieving scalability with incremental deployment.
sections.eli5: A multi-area network can have a few central routers that relay all the routing information instead of every router talking to every other router directly. This keeps the control plane simple while allowing data to still take many different paths.

sections.title: Flood Reflectors and Adjacencies
sections.content:
A flood reflector is a router configured to connect in Level 2 only to flood reflector clients and to reflood (repeat) Level 2 Link State Protocol Data Units (LSPs) it receives. A flood reflector client is a Level 1/Level 2 border router configured to build adjacencies only to flood reflectors within its area, not to other clients or external Level 2 nodes.

A flood reflection adjacency is a Level 2 adjacency between a client and a reflector within the same cluster, identified by a cluster ID. The cluster ID is a 32-bit value assigned to all flood reflectors and clients in the same Level 1 area. Routers verify that adjacencies form only between a client and a reflector with matching cluster IDs, ensuring the correct topology. Multiple flood reflectors can exist in a single cluster for redundancy; they do not need to synchronize with each other beyond normal IS-IS flooding.

From the perspective of Level 2 routers outside the transit area, the flood reflector adjacencies appear as normal Level 2 links. The LSPs flooded by the reflector reach all reachable networks, allowing Level 2 computation to find paths through the transit area without knowing its internal structure. This abstraction is the basis for scalability.
sections.eli5: Flood reflectors are routers that relay routing messages. Clients connect only to reflectors, not to each other. All clients in the same area use the same cluster ID so routers know which ones belong together.

sections.title: Tunnel-Based and No-Tunnel Deployments
sections.content:
The RFC defines two forwarding modes: tunnel-based and no-tunnel. In tunnel-based mode, border routers build tunnels across the Level 1 area to shortcut traffic that would otherwise traverse only the flood reflector. A client can build tunnels to the flood reflector and to other clients, creating a partial or full mesh of tunnels at the Level 1 layer. These tunnels appear in the Level 1 topology and carry data traffic, allowing forwarding to use the entire Level 1 topology rather than concentrating traffic at the reflector.

In no-tunnel mode, clients redistribute Level 2 reachability information into Level 1, allowing other clients and Level 1 routers to discover Level 2 destinations via the Level 1 routing. This avoids the need to build and manage tunnels but requires careful scoping of reachability to avoid routing loops and suboptimal paths.

Both modes allow Level 1 routers (non-border routers) to remain unchanged and unaware of flood reflection. Clients also need not be aware of the specific tunneling technology; the RFC provides a general mechanism for auto-discovering tunnel endpoints and parameters, allowing implementations to choose whether to establish tunnels statically or dynamically.
sections.eli5: Data can take two paths through a flood reflection cluster: either through actual tunnels that bypass the reflector, or by redistributing the network information into Level 1 so routers can find alternate paths.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Incremental Deployment
sections.content:
A key advantage of flood reflection is that it is backward-compatible with existing IS-IS implementations. Standard IS-IS routers outside the flood reflection cluster do not need any changes. They see the flood reflector adjacencies as normal Level 2 links and compute shortest paths using them as they would with any other adjacency. Only routers directly participating in flood reflection (flood reflectors and clients) need to be upgraded.

This backward compatibility enables incremental deployment: network operators can upgrade some routers to support flood reflection and configure them as reflectors or clients without requiring a simultaneous upgrade of the entire network. Over time, additional Level 1 areas can be converted to flood reflection clusters, progressively improving the scalability of the network.

However, the RFC notes that flood reflection may cause suboptimal routing paths in some scenarios. Because the Level 2 topology is simplified, the Level 2 shortest path computation may choose paths that appear optimal at the Level 2 level but are not globally optimal. This is a deliberate trade-off between control plane scalability and path optimality, similar to issues in BGP route reflection.
sections.eli5: Flood reflection can be added to a network without upgrading all routers at once. Old routers just see the new adjacencies as normal links, while new routers understand the special flood reflection topology.

sections.title: New TLVs and Encodings
sections.content:
Flood reflection introduces three new TLVs (Type-Length-Value fields) to IS-IS messages. The Flood Reflection TLV is included in Level 2 Hello (IIH) messages on flood reflection adjacencies. It carries the cluster ID and a bit indicating whether the router is a flood reflector or a client, ensuring that adjacencies form only between correctly configured routers.

The Flood Reflection Discovery sub-TLV is carried in the Router Capability TLV and is flooded in both Level 1 and Level 2 LSPs. It allows routers outside the transit area to discover which adjacencies are flood reflection adjacencies and enables auto-discovery of tunnel endpoints across the cluster.

The Flood Reflection Adjacency sub-TLV is included in neighbor information TLVs to mark a specific adjacency as a flood reflection adjacency. When Level 2 nodes outside the cluster receive and process these TLVs, they can recognize flood reflection clusters and annotate the topology accordingly.

Optional tunnel discovery sub-TLVs allow encapsulation types and tunnel endpoint information to be advertised, enabling automatic tunnel establishment. The RFC does not mandate any specific tunneling technology; implementations may use whatever tunneling mechanism is suitable and configured.
sections.eli5: The protocol adds special labels to messages to identify flood reflector nodes, mark flood reflection adjacencies, and provide tunnel information for automatic path setup.
